papers.title: Multi-Target Wireless Localization of Miniaturized Magneto-Oscillatory Trackers in Soft Biological Tissues.
papers.abstract: Accurate lesion localization is essential for precision medicine applications such as radiation therapy and minimally invasive surgery. However, preoperative imaging often fails to represent intraoperative anatomy because of surgical repositioning and physiological motion, highlighting the need for a wireless, radiation-free tracking approach with real-time positional feedback. Here, we present miniaturized wireless trackers based on a small-scale magneto-oscillatory localization (SMOL) method for multi-target localization in soft tissues. Distinct resonance frequencies are achieved using micro-resonators with different cantilevers and numbers of attached micro-magnets, enabling simultaneous identification and tracking. An optimized excitation strategy using three electromagnetic coils and a multi-step search scheme allows localization without prior target position or orientation information. The system achieves sub-millimeter precision and accuracy below 2 mm at distances up to 115 mm. Continuous tracking of three independent trackers was demonstrated in soft tissue phantoms and ex vivo porcine liver tissue. In addition, oscillation damping behavior indicates potential for rheological sensing of soft tissues. These wireless miniaturized trackers show strong potential for real-time localization in computer-assisted interventions.

papers.title: Utility of the CapsoCam Plus for Overt Gastrointestinal Bleeding After Negative Gastroscopy: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
papers.abstract:
Introduction

Patients with upper gastrointestinal bleeding have a nondiagnostic gastroscopy if bleeding is distal to the duodenum. Capsule endoscopy can localise bleeding to anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract; yield is highest when performed as soon as possible, although impaired motility in unwell patients reduces complete examination rate. The CapsoCam Plus operates without external support equipment, and has a long battery life, theoretically improving completion rate and diagnostic yield.

Objectives

The objectives were to determine the examination completion rate (to the caecum), diagnostic yield and impact on management of the CapsoCam Plus in patients with suspected acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding and nondiagnostic gastroscopy.

Methods

This was an observational retrospective cohort study of patients who underwent gastroscopy within 24 hours of admission to Sheffield Teaching Hospitals, with suspected upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Capsule endoscopy using the CapsoCam Plus was performed in those in whom gastroscopy was normal or identified lesions of uncertain significance. A single expert video reader identified and localised blood, pathological lesions, completeness of small bowel examination and duration of examination. Data were collected retrospectively, including the nature of bleeding, type and timing of investigations, management and diagnosis.

Results

A median of 9 days (IQR 5-14 days) after bleeding, 113 capsule endoscopies were performed in 106 patients (62 M, median age 72 (IQR 63-79) years). Examination was complete to the caecum in 96.5% of cases. Capsule endoscopy identified pathology, blood (in the upper gastrointestinal tract [5.6%], small bowel [68.4%], colon [24.1%] or throughout [1.9%]) or both in 54 (47.8%) examinations, guiding further investigation in 30 (55.6%) of these cases. Of the total number of examinations, capsule endoscopy alone or following guided investigation led to new diagnoses in 21 (18.6%, mostly in the small bowel) and therapeutic intervention in 18 (15.9%).

Conclusions

CapsoCam capsule endoscopy had a high completion rate, making new diagnoses in 18.6% of patients and altering management in the majority of this subgroup.

papers.title: GBS-MeDIP: A method for the simultaneous identification of genetic and epigenetic variants in tumors.
papers.abstract: Tumor development arises from combined genetic and epigenetic alterations, yet most sequencing approaches examine these layers independently. We present GBS-MeDIP, a low-input and cost-efficient method that combines genotype-by-sequencing with methylated DNA immunoprecipitation to jointly identify single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), copy number variations (CNVs), and differentially methylated regions (DMRs) within the same genomic fraction. The method was evaluated in two clinical contexts: gastric adenocarcinoma (a malignant epithelial tumor) and parathyroid adenoma (a benign endocrine tumor). In both case studies, we detected thousands of SNPs, with principal component analysis (PCA) revealing genetic divergence in gastric tumors and substantial inter-individual genetic background differences in parathyroid samples. We identified many CNVs in both datasets, with CNVs more frequent in parathyroid tumors, showing a stronger representation in promoter regions than SNPs. Gastric cancer showed a balanced methylation profile, with four DMRs reaching false discovery rate (FDR) significance, whereas Mimpara-treated parathyroid tumors displayed widespread hypermethylation, with all significant DMRs hypermethylated. These significant DMRs mapped to genes involved in immune regulation, chromatin function, DNA repair, and endocrine signaling. Annotation analysis demonstrated that, in both tissues, CNVs were enriched in promoter and exonic regions, whereas DMRs were preferentially located in intronic and intergenic regions, reflecting the CpG-enriched reduced genomic fraction accessed by GBS-MeDIP. Importantly, both datasets contained DMRs overlapping CNVs, highlighting the method's ability to reveal genetic confounders in methylation studies. Together, these results show that GBS-MeDIP enables combined genomic and epigenomic profiling in heterogeneous clinical tumor samples.

papers.title: Synchronous ipsilateral clear cell renal cell carcinoma and upper tract urothelial carcinoma complicated by ureteral stone: a case report.
papers.abstract: Synchronous renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and upper tract urothelial carcinoma (UTUC) in one renal unit are rare and diagnostically challenging. A 52-year-old man with flank pain and hematuria had an enhancing renal mass, hydronephrosis, ureteral wall thickening, impaired excretion, and an obstructing ureteral stone. Magnetic resonance imaging suggested synchronous RCC and UTUC. Laparoscopic radical nephroureterectomy with bladder cuff excision and left renal hilar lymph-node sampling revealed WHO/ISUP grade 2 clear cell RCC (pT1aN0) and low-grade invasive UTUC (pT1N0). At 6 months, imaging and cystoscopic biopsies showed no recurrence. Imaging raised suspicion of synchronous malignancies, while histopathology confirmed both diagnoses and demonstrated less extensive UTUC than suggested radiologically.

papers.title: Subtype-resolved tumor-intrinsic programs in immune-cold breast cancer: mechanistic interactions, evidence gaps, and translational priorities.
papers.abstract: Most breast cancers respond poorly to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB), and hormone receptor-positive (HR +) tumors, which constitute most diagnoses, are particularly refractory. This review synthesizes evidence on tumor-intrinsic determinants of the immune-cold phenotype in breast cancer under an operational framework designated ICE, comprising three functionally defined domains: Invisibility (failure of antigen generation, presentation, and innate sensing), Coercion (active exclusion and post-infiltration suppression of effector cells), and Exhaustion-by-Metabolism (metabolic attrition of infiltrating lymphocytes). ICE is not proposed as a newly discovered taxonomy of immune evasion; its added value lies in integrating breast-cancer subtype resolution, evidence provenance, systems-level interactions, negative clinical evidence, and mechanism-biomarker-intervention matching within a single operational framework. Four features define this framework. The domains are overlapping rather than sequential, and an explicit assignment rule places multifunctional regulators such as MYC, hypoxia-inducible factor 1α, and lactate in a primary domain while cataloguing secondary effects. Tumor-immune interaction is treated as bidirectional, positioning tumor-intrinsic programs as both causes and consequences of immune pressure. Major mechanistic and translational claims are assigned claim-specific evidence tiers. Resistance to immune-mediated killing, including death receptor loss, is classified as cross-dimensional cytoprotection rather than a recognition defect. Applying this discipline exposes an asymmetric evidence base: antigen presentation defects and metabolic suppression rest on substantial preclinical data with limited clinical validation, several widely cited mechanisms derive from non-breast models, and the translational record includes cross-cancer constraints-failure of IDO1 inhibition in a melanoma phase III trial and minimal STING-agonist monotherapy activity in early mixed-solid-tumor studies-together with breast-cancer-specific negative findings from IMpassion131 and the unfavorable benefit-risk profile of abemaciclib plus pembrolizumab. Cross-dimensional systems-level structures, including the hypoxia-adenylosuccinate lyase-fumarate-STING axis and the tumor-macrophage arginine-polyamine relay, are identified as the most instructive examples of domain interaction, and seven falsifiable predictions are advanced, each specifying a measurable biomarker and a decisive experiment.

papers.title: Impaired discrimination of negative facial emotions in pure motor ALS.
papers.abstract:
Background and objectives

Emotion recognition deficits in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) remain debated. We investigated whether patients with pure motor ALS (without cognitive and behavioural disturbances) and without clinically relevant mood disturbances are impaired in discriminating negative facial emotions, using a test without ceiling effects.

Methods

This cross-sectional study included 35 patients with pure motor ALS, based on the revised Strong criteria and operationalised using the Edinburgh Cognitive and Behavioural ALS Screen (ECAS), without clinically relevant mood disturbances, alongside 35 age-, sex-, and education-matched cognitively and psychiatrically healthy controls. All participants completed a shortened five-emotion version of the Facial Emotion Intensity Rating Test - Congruent and Incongruent and the Facial Sex Matching Task (FSMT), a brief screening measure of non-emotional facial discrimination.

Results

Pure motor ALS patients showed poorer discrimination among negative facial emotions than healthy controls (p = 0.011, Cohen's d = 0.63). The group difference did not differ significantly across anger, fear, sadness, and disgust (p = 0.178). Similarly, the group difference in discrimination among negative emotions did not differ significantly from that in discrimination between negative emotions and happiness (p = 0.459). The two groups did not differ significantly on the FSMT.

Conclusion

Discrimination of negative facial emotions was impaired in patients with pure motor ALS, suggesting that classification based on ECAS screening may underestimate social-cognitive involvement. Our findings are compatible with the concept of an ALS-frontotemporal spectrum disorder. Whether impaired emotion discrimination relates to additional cognitive or behavioural impairment remains to be determined. The clinical utility and reliability of our measure require further study.

papers.title: Fruquintinib Plus FOLFIRI/FOLFOX as Second-Line Therapy in Patients With RAS-Mutant Metastatic Colorectal Cancer: A Multicenter, Open-Label, Single-Arm Phase II Study.
papers.abstract: For patients with RAS-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC), effective second-line therapies remain limited. In this multicenter, single-arm phase II trial conducted from March 2023 to November 2025, we enrolled 42 patients with RAS-mutant mCRC who had progressed after first-line therapy. All patients received fruquintinib (4 mg once daily on Days 1-21 of each 28-day cycle) combined with either FOLFIRI or FOLFOX chemotherapy based on prior treatment history. The median progression-free survival (PFS) was 8.08 months (95% CI: 6.18, 9.46), ranking among the longest reported in the second-line setting. The objective response rate (ORR) was 52.5% (95% CI: 36.13, 68.49) and the disease control (DCR) rate 97.5% (95% CI: 86.84, 99.94). Notably, this study reports the first conversion surgery outcomes in this setting, with three patients (7.14%) undergoing successful resection-a rate approaching that observed in first-line trials. The safety profile was manageable, with 7.1% of patients experiencing grade ≥ 3 adverse events including diarrhea (4.8%) and thrombocytopenia (2.4%); no treatment-related deaths occurred. Prior bevacizumab treatment did not affect the consistent efficacy of this regimen. These results support further randomized evaluation of this fruquintinib-based combination as a promising second-line option for patients with RAS-mutant mCRC.

papers.title: High tissue factor (CD142) expression identifies a poor-prognosis subgroup of esophageal and esophagogastric junction adenocarcinoma.
papers.abstract:
Background

Tissue Factor (TF/CD142) is an emerging antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) target, but its prevalence, prognostic value and molecular context in adenocarcinoma of the esophagus (EAC) and esophagogastric junction (EGJ) remain uncharacterized.

Methods

TF immunohistochemistry was scored by H-score (0-300) on a tissue microarray of 1,120 resected EAC/EGJ adenocarcinomas (1996-2020); the 1,006 assessable primary tumors formed the analysis cohort. Tumors were graded TF-negative (≤ 10), TF-low (11-100) or TF-high (> 100) and related to clinicopathologic features, tissue compartment, neoadjuvant therapy, HER2, Claudin 18.2 (CLDN18.2), MET, mismatch-repair (MMR) status and overall survival. Primary tumors and lymph-node metastases were compared within patients.

Results

TF was positive in 486 of 1,006 tumors (48.3%) and high in 225 (22.4%). TF-positive tumors were more often pT3-4 (p < 0.001) and node-positive (p = 0.002), and TF grade agreed moderately between paired primary tumors and lymph-node metastases (n = 247; κ 0.57 at H-score > 100) without a systematic shift (p = 0.91). TF was independent of HER2 (p = 0.80) and MMR status (p = 0.14), inversely associated with CLDN18.2 (TF-high vs. TF-negative: 12.8% vs. 30.2%; p < 0.001) and positively with MET overexpression (8.6% vs. 1.0%; p < 0.001). Over a median follow-up of 67 months (749 patients, 428 deaths), the survival detriment was confined to TF-high tumors (median overall survival 19.3 vs. 36.8 and 42.2 months; p < 0.001). Adjusted for age, pT, nodal status and neoadjuvant therapy, TF-high remained adverse (HR 1.67, 95% CI 1.32-2.11; p < 0.001) whereas TF-low did not (HR 0.97; p = 0.83). The TF-high association held with TF as a continuous variable (HR 1.11 per 50 points; p < 0.001) and after adjustment for treatment era, margin, grade and lymphovascular invasion. TF positivity was similar in treatment-naïve and in residual post-neoadjuvant tumors (p = 0.89), but TF-high concentrated in poorly regressed tumors (29.2% vs. 11.6%; trend p < 0.001).

Conclusions

TF is expressed in nearly half of EAC/EGJ adenocarcinomas and at high level in about one quarter, where it is independently associated with shorter overall survival. TF expression remains prevalent in residual tumors after neoadjuvant therapy and marks a compartment distinct from HER2 and CLDN18.2 and enriched for MET. TF-high is a candidate biomarker for prospective trials of TF-directed ADCs, in which its predictive value and the H-score > 100 threshold need testing.

papers.title: Spatial transcriptomics tumor microenvironment determinants of tyrosine kinase inhibitor response in renal cell carcinoma: results from a phase 2 clinical trial.
papers.abstract: Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) exhibits heterogeneous clinical outcomes, and limited biomarkers are available to predict response to targeted therapies. This study evaluated cell compartment-specific transcriptional biomarkers predicting clinical response to the tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) sunitinib. In this phase 2 clinical trial (NCT00715442), 46 patients with metastatic ccRCC received sunitinib pre- and post-cytoreductive nephrectomy, with a primary endpoint of time-to-progression (TTP) and secondary endpoints of overall survival (OS) and sunitinib toxicity. To investigate spatial dynamics of therapeutic response to sunitinib, we applied whole-transcriptome digital spatial profiling (DSP) to tumor tissue from responders and non-responders. For 46 trial patients, median TTP was 8.2 months (95% CI: 6.1-19.3) and OS 36.3 months (95% CI: 19.7-70.5). Responders displayed a tumor microenvironment enriched in pro-inflammatory/immunostimulatory programs, while non-responders displayed enrichment of immunosuppressive programs with elevated PD-L1 expression in myeloid cells and exhausted CD8 + T-cell signatures. Sunitinib resistance mechanisms involving VEGF-dependent and independent angiogenic pathways were identified, revealing potential therapeutic targets. DSP-based machine learning models showed strong prognostic and predictive performance in sunitinib-treated patients in an external JAVELIN Renal 101 cohort, but attenuated performance in the avelumab plus axitinib cohort, indicating treatment-context specificity. Our findings highlight immune regulation as a key determinant of sunitinib response in metastatic ccRCC. Spatial profiling revealed potentially targetable mechanisms of TKI resistance involving SPP1-associated myeloid programs, CD8 + T-cell exhaustion, and angiogenic signaling, highlighting interactions between angiogenesis, lipid metabolism, and tumor immunity as determinants of therapeutic outcome.

papers.title: A Bioengineered Mitochondrial Respiration-Mimetic Copper-Based Metal-Organic Framework Reprogramming Oxidative Phosphorylation to Enhance Tumor Cuproptosis.
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial metabolism-dependent cuproptosis has emerged as a promising anticancer modality, yet its efficacy is constrained by the hypoxic and glycolysis-dominant tumor microenvironment that suppresses oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). Strategies that simultaneously overcome hypoxia and mitochondrial metabolic resistance remain underexplored. Herein, we report a bioengineered mitochondrial respiration-mimetic nanoplatform (TC@OMG) that renews tumor mitochondrial metabolism to enhance cuproptosis. TC@OMG integrates a copper-based metal-organic framework co-loaded with glucose oxidase and a lactate dehydrogenase inhibitor, and is cloaked with a hybrid membrane derived from tumor cells and plant thylakoids, enabling tumor targeting and photosynthetic oxygen generation. Mechanistically, photo-triggered TC@OMG couples hypoxia alleviation with glycolysis inhibition to enforce a metabolic shift toward mitochondrial OXPHOS, thereby sensitizing tumor cells to cuproptosis. Concurrently, its microenvironment-responsive copper release and glutathione depletion disrupt mitochondrial Fe-S cluster homeostasis and induce aggregation of lipoylated proteins, ultimately promoting cuproptotic cell death. In vivo, photo-triggered TC@OMG achieves efficient tumor targeting, hypoxia relieving, and tumor inhibiting effects across multiple melanoma models, including subcutaneous, metastatic, and intraocular tumors. Collectively, this work bioengineered a respiration-mimetic nanotherapeutic strategy that integrates mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming with copper-dependent cell death, providing a generalizable strategy for overcoming mitochondrial metabolic resistance in cancer therapy.

papers.title: Combined Immunotherapy and Hybrid Dose-Fraction Radiotherapy for Driver-Negative Metastatic NSCLC: A Phase II Trial with Parallel Preclinical Studies.
papers.abstract: Background: Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-based chemoimmunotherapy has become a standard first-line treatment for patients with driver-negative metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but the clinical benefit is limited. Radiotherapy has potential antitumor immunomodulatory effects, but the optimal dose and fractionation remain unclear. Methods: This single-arm, multicenter, prospective, phase II trial enrolled patients with stage IV driver-negative NSCLC who received first-line chemoimmunotherapy. During the ICI maintenance phase, patients received hybrid dose-fraction radiotherapy (Hybrid-RT): stereotactic ablative body radiotherapy (SABR) to targetable lesions and low-dose radiotherapy (LDRT) to other sites. Patients restaged to stage III disease after chemoimmunotherapy received short-course hypofractionated radiotherapy to all residual lesions. The primary endpoint was 1-year progression-free survival (PFS) rate. The secondary endpoints included 1-year overall survival (OS) rate, objective response rate, and safety. Parallel preclinical mechanistic studies were performed in a murine model. Results: A total of 83 patients were enrolled from 2022 May 9 to 2023 December 31. The 1-year PFS rate was 54.2% (median PFS 16.1 months; 95% confidence interval [CI] 11.4 to 19.2 months), meeting the primary endpoint. The 1-year OS rate was 83.1% (median OS 29.3 months; 95% CI 21.9 months to not reached), and treatment was well tolerated. Peripheral immune profiling showed posttreatment expansion of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and natural killer (NK) cells associated with promising clinical efficacy. In the murine model, ICI plus Hybrid-RT (IHBRT) induced a division of labor between CD8+ T and NK cells. At LDRT lesions, it facilitated both C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 3 (Cxcr3)-mediated recruitment of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and natural killer group 2 member D-mediated NK cell cytotoxicity. At SABR lesions, Cxcr3-mediated CD8+ T cells played a predominant role, whereas NK cells contributed minimally. Moreover, IHBRT suppressed secreted phosphoprotein 1 positive (Spp1+) macrophages and relieved immunosuppression. Conclusions: Clinically, IHBRT demonstrates promising efficacy and a manageable safety profile in driver-negative metastatic NSCLC. Preclinically, it induces a functional division of labor between CD8+ T and NK cells to activate antitumor immune cytotoxicity, and suppresses Spp1+ macrophages, thereby relieving immunosuppression. Trial registration: This trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT05348668). Date of registration: 2022 April 26.

papers.title: Multimodal single-cell analyses reveal distinct fusion-regulated transcriptional programs in Ewing sarcoma.
papers.abstract: Ewing sarcoma (EwS) is a fusion-driven malignancy, peaking in adolescence. Although EwS tumors are driven uniquely by EWS::FLI1 and related fusions, patient outcomes vary greatly. If and how tumor plasticity of EWS::FLI1-regulated transcriptional signatures contributes to disease progression is not known. To address this, we utilized a single-cell co-assay of RNA and chromatin accessibility (ATAC) sequencing to identify gene regulatory networks in EwS. By comprehensively characterizing regulatory elements across cell lines, we identified multiple unique modules of gene regulation. Differential usage and prevalence of these modules was evident across cell lines, associated with distinct epigenetic and transcriptomic signatures, and in specific cases, modifiable by exogenous TGF-β. When we examined primary EwS patient tumors, we observed these same regulatory modules were variably enriched both across and within tumors, highlighting the existence of intratumoral heterogeneity in gene regulatory networks. Our findings demonstrate that multiple, co-existing transcriptional programs shape the phenotypic diversity of EwS and suggest that the balance between these networks may have important implications for clinical outcomes and targeted therapy development.

papers.title: Cell death: from basic principles to translational developments.
papers.abstract: The precise regulation of cell death is indispensable for embryonic development, tissue homeostasis, and the pathophysiology of human disease. Dysfunctions in regulated cell death (RCD) pathways constitute a critical aetiological factor in diverse pathologies, including oncogenesis, neurodegenerative disorders, autoimmune conditions, and ischaemic injury. Substantial efforts to therapeutically target these mechanisms are therefore needed. In this review, we present a systematic analysis of the molecular machinery underlying distinct RCD processes, including apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, and multiple forms of metal-dependent cell death. We delineate how the interconnected signalling networks that govern these pathways are coordinated at the cellular and organismal levels and how their dysregulation drives disease progression. We also emphasise translating mechanistic insights into clinical practice by critically evaluating pharmacological strategies. Furthermore, this review systematically describes how an improved understanding of pathway crosstalk mechanisms, the discovery of predictive biomarkers, and advances in targeted delivery systems collectively drive the development of precision therapeutic strategies. Finally, we discuss current challenges in achieving on-target specificity and minimising off-tumour toxicity, and we outline future directions for integrating these approaches into immunomodulatory and combination frameworks. By bridging fundamental cell biology with translational medicine, this review aims to illuminate both the conceptual foundations and the clinical potential of targeting cell death in human diseases.

papers.title: Somatostatin receptor-targeted DOTATATE PET/CT in breast cancer and breast lesions: a systematic review of detection, incidental findings and theranostic potential
papers.abstract: Background Somatostatin receptor 2 (SSTR2) is expressed by a subset of breast cancers, particularly oestrogen receptor (ER)-positive tumours. DOTATATE PET/CT, the reference standard for neuroendocrine tumour (NET) imaging, is increasingly relevant to breast cancer staging, incidental findings and theranostic selection. We systematically reviewed its clinical performance. Methods Following PRISMA 2020 (PROSPERO CRD420261508548), Embase, Scopus and PubMed were searched to 16 September 2026, supplemented by citation searching. Studies reporting DOTATATE PET findings in breast cancer or breast lesions were included. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2 and Joanna Briggs Institute tools, certainty with GRADE, and findings were synthesised narratively. Results Nineteen studies (four prospective, two retrospective cohorts, three case series, ten case reports) including 107 patients with breast carcinoma were analysed. In head-to-head comparisons (n = 56), DOTATATE detected disease in most patients and matched 18 F-FDG for skeletal (252 vs 255 lesions) and nodal metastases, but identified half as many visceral metastases (134 vs 262), particularly in the liver. Uptake favoured ER-positive, lobular and neuroendocrine tumours. Focal breast uptake occurred on 1.1% of scans performed for other indications; 21.4% of characterised lesions were malignant and SUVmax did not discriminate benign from malignant lesions. Krenning scores ≥ 3 were found in 15/76 (19.7%) patients across three prospective studies. Certainty of evidence was very low. Conclusions DOTATATE PET/CT complements, but cannot replace, 18 F-FDG for breast cancer staging, and is less established than 18 F-FES. Incidental breast uptake warrants standard breast work-up regardless of intensity. Around one-fifth of patients with ER-positive metastatic disease show high SSTR expression, although whether this has therapeutic relevance remains uncertain.

papers.title: High AXL Expression and Stromal-Angiogenic Immune Phenotypes in Upper Gastrointestinal Cancers.
papers.abstract: AXL, a receptor tyrosine kinase, has been implicated in epithelial-mesenchymal transition, angiogenesis, immune evasion, and therapeutic resistance, but its relevance in upper gastrointestinal cancers remains incompletely defined. We analyzed 337 patients with advanced gastric (n = 287) or esophageal (n = 50) cancer enrolled in SCRUM-Japan MONSTAR-SCREEN-2, whose tumors were profiled by whole-exome and whole-transcriptome sequencing. Patients were classified as AXL-high (n = 169) or AXL-low (n = 168) using cancer type-specific median transcripts-per-million cutoffs. Median follow-up was 14.1 months. AXL-high tumors were associated with shorter overall survival than AXL-low tumors (median, 12.9 versus 17.1 months; hazard ratio, 1.58; 95% confidence interval, 1.17-2.14; p = 0.003), consistently in gastric (hazard ratio, 1.47; p = 0.020) and esophageal (hazard ratio, 2.46; p = 0.027) cancer. This association persisted after adjustment for cancer type, age, sex, number of metastatic sites, microsatellite instability status, and tumor mutational burden (hazard ratio, 1.59; 95% confidence interval, 1.14-2.22; p = 0.007). Among microsatellite stable patients treated with immune checkpoint blockade, AXL expression was not associated with progression-free survival (hazard ratio, 0.83; 95% confidence interval, 0.61-1.14; p = 0.255). AXL-high tumors showed stromal and vascular expansion, regulatory T-cell enrichment, higher expression of fibroblast growth factor receptor 1, vascular endothelial growth factor receptors 1-3, and MET, and enrichment of epithelial-mesenchymal transition, angiogenesis, and transforming growth factor beta signaling. High AXL expression identifies a poor-prognosis stromal-angiogenic phenotype in upper gastrointestinal cancers and warrants prospective validation as a prognostic, rather than predictive, biomarker. Trial Registration: UMIN Clinical Trials Registry, UMIN000043899.

papers.title: Integrative transcriptomic and functional analyses reveal that ANXA3 suppresses tumor progression in SCLC-N by attenuating a neural transcriptional program.
papers.abstract: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a highly aggressive neuroendocrine malignancy with substantial molecular heterogeneity. SCLC-N is characterized by high NEUROD1 expression and associated neural transcriptional activity, yet its intra-subtype heterogeneity and molecular correlates remain poorly understood. We integrated single-cell and bulk transcriptomic analyses with experimental validation to characterize intra-subtype neural transcriptional heterogeneity and identify candidate genes. Consensus non-negative matrix factorization identified 12 transcriptional programs, including a neural transcriptional program (NTP) whose activity varied continuously across malignant SCLC-N cells. NTP activity was closely associated with NEUROD1 expression and inferred regulatory activity and correlated reproducibly with an independent NEUROD1 associated transcriptional signature across multiple cohorts. Higher NTP scores were associated with transcriptional features related to malignancy and poorer overall survival. Integrative analyses focusing on genes negatively correlated with NTP activity prioritized ANXA3 as a candidate gene. ANXA3 was downregulated in SCLC, and lower ANXA3 expression was associated with enrichment of transcriptional programs related to the cell cycle. ANXA3 overexpression reduced NEUROD1 expression and attenuated NTP activity and related neural transcriptional features, while suppressing cell proliferation and xenograft tumor growth. NEUROD1 restoration partially rescued the antiproliferative effects of ANXA3 overexpression, while RNA-seq analysis further supported the recovery of NTP activity. Collectively, these findings reveal neural transcriptional heterogeneity within SCLC-N and demonstrate that ANXA3 overexpression suppresses tumor growth and attenuates NTP activity, with NEUROD1 restoration providing further support for a functional link between NTP attenuation and reduced cell proliferation.

papers.title: Multidisciplinary management of disseminated tuberculosis with tuberculous meningitis and active hepatitis B in a critically ill pregnant woman in the third trimester: a case report.
papers.abstract:
Background

Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) in pregnancy is rare but life-threatening, with substantial maternal and fetal risks. Third-trimester disseminated tuberculosis involving the central nervous system with concurrent active hepatitis B infection has scarcely been reported, particularly among remote pastoral populations with limited healthcare access. This report highlights the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges of this triple comorbidity and underscores the value of multidisciplinary team (MDT) management in such complex scenarios.

Case presentation

A 24-year-old pastoralist at 30 weeks of gestation presented with headache, vomiting, fever, and nuchal rigidity. Cerebrospinal fluidanalysis confirmed TBM, and chest computed tomography revealed diffuse miliary nodules suggestive of hematogenous disseminated tuberculosis. Serology was positive for hepatitis B surface antigen, e-antigen, and core antibody, indicating active viral replication. Given life-threatening intracranial hypertension [intracranial pressure (ICP) > 330 mmH2O] in late pregnancy, osmotic agents were withheld for fetal safety, and lumbar cisternal drainage was performed. An MDT comprising respiratory medicine, obstetrics, hepatology, pharmacy, and critical care nursing specialties was assembled. Anti-tuberculosis therapy was intensified to isoniazid, rifampicin, linezolid, and moxifloxacin; ethambutol was discontinued due to fetal optic neuritis, and tenofovir was added for hepatitis B management. Following stabilization, the patient was transferred to a higher-level facility at 35 weeks of gestation and underwent cesarean section at 36 weeks, delivering a live preterm female infant (2320 g, 1-min Apgar score of 8). Both mother and neonate were discharged without complications on December 1, 2025.

Conclusions

This case demonstrates that early recognition, individualized anti-tuberculosis regimens, and coordinated multidisciplinary collaboration are critical for achieving favorable outcomes in pregnant patients with disseminated tuberculosis complicated by TBM and concurrent hepatitis B infection. The successful management relied on integrated critical care and a multidisciplinary approach, which proved effective even in resource-limited pastoral settings.

papers.title: Perceived occupational physical fitness priorities and a preliminary conceptual framework for information technology students at selected vocational colleges in Shanxi Province, China: An exploratory cross-sectional mixed-methods study.
papers.abstract: Students majoring in information technology are frequently exposed to prolonged sitting, continuous screen use, sustained static postures, repetitive fine motor operations, and high cognitive load during their academic training and future work. These conditions may increase the risk of visual fatigue, neck and lower-back discomfort, physical fatigue, and psychological stress. This study adopted an exploratory cross-sectional mixed-methods design, using questionnaire surveys as the primary method and semi-structured interviews as a supplementary method. Participants included information technology students from selected vocational colleges, teachers whose teaching or research activities were related to vocational education or information technology student training, and personnel from information technology-related enterprises in Shanxi Province, China. The final analytical sample comprised 1,924 questionnaires: 1,863 from students, 37 from teachers, and 24 from enterprise personnel. The results showed that 68.71% of students selected "Frequently" or "Occasionally" when asked about physical discomfort following professional practical operations such as prolonged computer use or equipment debugging. The most frequently selected physical-discomfort categories included dry eyes or blurred vision, cervical or lumbar soreness, physical fatigue, and insufficient endurance. Weekly exercise duration was most commonly reported as 1-3 h/week (52.01%), whereas 14.76% of students selected "Almost no exercise." Qualitative interviews with students and teachers further suggested limited incorporation of occupation-specific training-such as visual relaxation and protection, musculoskeletal relaxation, postural adjustment, and sedentary behavior interruption-into current educational practice. The teacher sample indicated perceived constraints related to limited access to job-demand information, the availability of occupation-specific training methods and teaching resources, and student engagement. The enterprise sample suggested that some enterprise personnel recognized the potential role of occupational physical fitness in job adaptation and work efficiency; however, their actual involvement in curriculum development and the provision of job-related standards remained limited. Based on literature analysis, expert content validity evaluation, questionnaire survey data, and interview data, this study proposed a preliminary conceptual framework for occupational physical fitness in information technology programs, consisting of general physical fitness, occupation-specific physical fitness, and psychological fitness. These findings provide preliminary contextual evidence that occupation-related curriculum content and school-enterprise collaboration may warrant further investigation in vocational-education contexts similar to those examined in this study. Because this study used convenience sampling, included relatively small teacher and enterprise samples, and has not yet verified the proposed framework through structural validity testing or objective measurements, the framework requires further examination in larger and more balanced samples.

papers.title: Cancer drug resistance as a temporal process: cell plasticity, adaptive buffering, signaling pathways and therapeutic interception.
papers.abstract: Cancer drug resistance remains a principal barrier to durable cancer control, yet it is still often interpreted through endpoint-centred models that emphasise pre-existing resistant clones, incomplete drug exposure or late-acquired mechanisms. These explanations are essential but incomplete. The question is not only why resistant cells exist, but also how residual cells remain alive long enough to become resistant. Across tumour types and therapeutic modalities, treatment reshapes residual populations while it is acting, driving transitions through non-genetic heterogeneity, stochastic cell-fate variability, reversible tolerance, stress adaptation, microenvironmental support and eventually stable resistance. This Review develops a temporal framework in which resistance is resolved into a phase-structured trajectory organised around two mechanistic transitions: entry into adaptive buffering and later stabilisation into resistance hardening. Adaptive buffering is defined operationally as a transient, support-dependent survival state in which residual tumour cells preserve viability by recruiting physiological support systems while molecular and phenotypic reorganisation proceeds. It is not a single pathway or a synonym for drug tolerance, but a functional demand-capacity state whose dependencies change over time. We distinguish adaptive buffering from drug tolerance, persister states, dormancy, minimal residual disease and established resistance and discuss how buffering can be evaluated experimentally using perturbational, single-cell, spatial, computational and functional readouts. The framework suggests that informative biomarkers should assign residual populations to adaptive phases, so that therapy can intercept transient dependencies before adaptive states become hardened and clinically entrenched.

trials.title: Tissue Procurement and Natural History Study of Neuroendocrine Neoplasms (NENs) Including Adrenocortical Carcinoma (ACC)
trials.conds: Neuroendocrine Tumors; Carcinoma, Neuroendocrine
trials.brief:
Background:

Neuroendocrine neoplasm (NENs)are rare cancers arising from the neuroendocrine cells and can affect almost any part of the body. They vary from low grade neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) to high grade neuroendocrine carcinomas (NECs). These tumors often occur in the gastrointestinal tract, pancreas, lungs, adrenal medulla (pheochromocytomas) or adrenal cortex (adrenocortical cancer) and other areas of the body mentioned below:

* Gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (GEP-NET): stomach, duodenum, pancreas, colon, appendix, etc.
* Liver and gallbladder
* Adrenal tumors
* Pituitary gland
* Thyroid gland: medullary thyroid carcinoma
* Parathyroid tumors
* Pulmonary neuroendocrine tumors: typical and atypical carcinoid, small cell lung cancer (SCLC), large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC)
* Extrapulmonary small cell cancer
* Peripheral nervous system tumors: paraganglioma, neuroblastoma)
* Breast and genitourinary tract

Their rates are rising in the United States and worldwide. Researchers want to learn more about NENs through this natural history study.

Objective:

To study the natural history of people with NENs and obtain samples from them to learn more about the disease. The clinical management of all NETs is not standardized, with only a few FDA-approved therapies and we would like to learn which combination therapeutic approach should be used, how long treatment should be continued, and in what subgroup of NENs a particular treatment option should be used.

Eligibility:

People aged 18 and older who have or are suspected to have NENs or ACC.

Design:

Participants will be screened with a medical history.

Participants will have a physical exam. Their symptoms and their ability to perform their normal activities will be reviewed. They will have blood and urine tests.

Participants will receive recommendations for managing their disease and potential treatment options. They will be able to ask as many questions as they would like.

Participants may provide saliva and blood, a for research. They will give tumor samples from a previous surgery or biopsy.

Participants may have optional biopsies. During biopsies, cancer tissue will be obtained using a needle and syringe. Tissue will be taken from the liver, lung, or a lymph node. Participants may have an imaging scan or ultrasound to help locate the tumor or area to be biopsied. They will receive local anesthesia and may be sedated.

Participants will complete a questionnaire about their family medical history.

Participants will have follow-up visits every 12 months. They will have physical exams and give samples. If their health changes, they may have extra visits. If they cannot visit NIH, they (or their doctor) will be contacted by phone or email.

Participants will take part in the study for all their life.

This study will evaluate members in families with a history of small bowel carcinoid cancer to study the natural history of those family members that have the disease, determine ways to improve early detection by performing surveillance on those at risk but without disease and to identify the gene(s) that may cause the tumors. Familial carcinoid tumors usually originate in hormone-producing cells that line the small intestine or other cells of the digestive tract. The tumors are slow-growing and usually take many years before they cause symptoms. It is known that these tumors occur more often in some families and are then passed from one generation to the next by inherited genes.

Members of families, including all siblings and offspring in which two or more immediate blood relatives have had small bowel carcinoid tumors are eligible for this study. In some cases unaffected spouses of family members diagnosed with carcinoid cancer are also requested to participate by donating a sample of blood only.

Participants undergo a medical evaluation every 3 years during a 3- to 5-day hospital stay at the NIH Clinical Center. All participants have a personal and family medical history obtained and undergo a physical examination, blood and urine tests.

People who already have a small bowel carcinoid tumor or are at risk of developing a carcinoid tumor have some or all of the following procedures to determine the presence of carcinoid tumor and its (omit next two words- location or) spread to other areas of the body:

* Video Capsule Endoscopy: Visualization of the gastrointestinal tract by ingesting a disposable, "vitamin-pill sized" video capsule that has its own camera and light source.
* CT of the chest abdomen and pelvis with oral and IV contrast : X-ray examination of the chest, abdominal and pelvis organs.
* 18 FDOPA Positron emission tomography (PET) with CT for localization: Nuclear imaging scan to look at tumor activity.
* MRI Liver with contrast - to determine if disease has spread to liver

trials.brief:
Background:

High-grade neuroendocrine carcinomas (HGNEC) are cancers that develop in different parts of the body, including the digestive tract, genitals, neck, and head. One drug (belinostat), combined with 2 other drugs (etoposide and cisplatin), is approved to treat HGNEC. But some people may have a gene variant that affects how quickly their body gets rid of the drug; these people may do better with different dosages of belinostat.

Objective:

To test higher or lower doses of belinostat based on gene variants in people with HGNEC.

Eligibility:

People aged 18 years and older with HGNEC.

Design:

Participants will be screened. They will have a physical exam with blood tests. Some blood will be used for genetic testing. They will have imaging scans and a test of their heart function. Samples of tumor tissue may be collected.

All 3 study drugs (belinostat, etoposide, cisplatin) are given through a tube attached to a needle inserted into a vein. Treatment will be given in 21-day cycles.

For cycles 1 through 6: Participants will come to the clinic for the first 4 days. They will be given all 3 drugs. Imaging scans and other tests will be repeated. Each visit will last 4 to 8 hours.

After cycle 6: Participants may continue treatment with belinostat alone. They will come to the clinic for the first 3 days of each cycle. They may continue treatment for up to 5 years if the drug is helping them.

Participants will have a follow-up visit 30 days after their last dose of belinostat. Then they will receive follow-up visits by phone or email every 3 to 6 months.

trials.brief:
Patients with digestive tract malignancy often experience severe and unremitting abdominal pain that negatively affects physical, emotional, and social function, as well as health related quality of life (HRQOL). Therapeutic virtual reality (VR) has emerged as a promising and evidence-based treatment modality for cancer pain. Users of VR wear a pair of goggles with a close-proximity screen in front of the eyes that creates a sensation of being transported into lifelike, three-dimensional worlds. To date, VR has been limited to short-term clinical trials for cancer pain. Moreover, limited research exists on theory-based VR modalities beyond mere distraction, such as VR that employs acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) with components of biofeedback and mindfulness. To bridge these gaps, this study seeks to: (1) assess the impact of immersive VR on patient-reported outcomes (PROs), including pain, activity metrics, and opioid use among patients with visceral pain from a digestive tract malignancy; (2) assess differences in PROs, activity metrics, and opioid use between skills-based VR therapy vs. distraction VR therapy; and (3) determine patient-level predictors of VR treatment response in visceral cancer pain.

To address these aims, the study will measure PROs and opioid use in 360 patients randomized among 3 groups and follow them for 60 days after enrollment: (1) an enhanced VR group receiving skills-based VR; (2) a distraction-based VR group receiving patient-selected VR videos; and (3) a VR sham control group using a VR headset with 2-D content. The results will inform best practices for the implementation of VR for visceral cancer pain management and guide selection of patient-tailored experiences.

trials.title: Comparing Retreatment of 177Lu-DOTATATE PRRT Versus the Usual Treatment in Patients With Metastatic Unresectable Gastroenteropancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors, NET RETREAT Trial

trials.brief: This phase II trial compares the effect of retreatment with 177Lu-DOTATATE peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) to the usual approach of treatment with everolimus, sunitinib, or cabozantinib in patients who have previously received 177Lu-DOTATATE for gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (GEPNET) that has spread from where it first started (primary site) to other places in the body (metastatic) and that cannot be removed by surgery (unresectable). PRRT is a type of radiation therapy for which a radioactive chemical is linked to a peptide (small protein) that targets tumor cells. When this radioactive peptide is injected into the body, it binds to a specific receptor found on some tumor cells. The radioactive peptide builds up in these cells and helps kill the tumor cells without harming normal cells. In this trial 177Lu-DOTATATE is used for PRRT. 177Lu-DOTATATE PRRT may increase the length of time until worsening of the GEPNET compared to the usual approach. Everolimus is in a class of medications called kinase inhibitors. It is also a type of angiogenesis inhibitor. Everolimus works by stopping tumor cells from reproducing and by decreasing blood supply to the tumor cells. Sunitinib and cabozantinib, block certain proteins, which may help keep tumor cells from growing. They may also prevent the growth of new blood vessels that tumors need to grow. Sunitinib malate is a type of tyrosine kinase inhibitor and a type of antiangiogenesis agent. Poly (adenosine diphosphate \[ADP\]-ribose) polymerases (PARPs) are proteins that help repair deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) mutations. PARP inhibitors, such as olaparib, can keep PARP from working, so tumor cells can't repair themselves, and they may stop growing. Chemotherapy drugs, such as temozolomide, work in different ways to stop the growth of tumor cells, either by killing the cells, by stopping them from dividing, or by stopping them from spreading. Giving olaparib with temozolomide may shrink or stabilize the cancer in patients with pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma better than temozolomide alone.

Background:

Neuroendocrine neoplasms (NENs) are rare cancers in the gastrointestinal tract, pancreas, lungs, adrenal glands, and other areas of the body. Many of these cancers have a high risk of relapse and a low chance of survival. Better treatments are needed.

Objective:

To test a new drug, ADCT-701, in people with NENs.

Eligibility:

Adults aged 18 and older with NENs.

Design:

Participants will be screened. They will have a physical exam with blood and urine tests. They will have imaging scans and tests of heart functioning. Their ability to perform normal daily activities will be tested. A biopsy may be needed: A sample of tissue will be removed from the tumor.

ADCT-701 is given through a tube attached to a needle inserted into a vein in the arm. Participants will receive the drug treatment on the first day of 21-day treatment cycles. They will visit the clinic a total of 10 times during the first two cycles. After that, they will visit the clinic 2 times during each cycle. Imaging scans, blood draws, heart function tests, and other tests will be repeated during study visits. Each visit will last up to 8 hours.

Participants may continue receiving treatment with the study drug for up to 2 years.

After treatment ends, participants will have follow-up clinic visits 4 times in 4 months. They will have a physical exam, with heart and blood tests, at each visit. After that, they will have follow-up clinic visits every 9 weeks; these visits will include imaging scans.

trials.brief:
Background:

Small cell carcinoma of the bladder (SCCB) and other high-grade neuroendocrine tumors (HGNET) of the urinary tract are rare but aggressive cancers. Average survival for people diagnosed with SCCB or HGNET is about 1 year. Lurbinectedin and avelumab are drugs that are approved to treat other cancers. Researchers want to see if these drugs can help people with SCCB or HGNET.

Objective:

To test lurbinectedin with or without avelumab in people with SCCB or HGNET.

Eligibility:

Adults aged 18 years and older with SCBB or HGNET that returned and spread after treatment.

Design:

Participants will be screened. They will have a physical exam. They will have blood tests and imaging scans. They may need to have a new biopsy: A small needle will be used to collect a tissue sample from the tumor.

Both study drugs are given through a tube attached to a needle inserted into a vein. If participants have already received a drug like avelumab they will receive only lurbinectedin. If patients have not been previously treated with a drug like avelumab they will receive both lurbinectedin and avelumab. All participants will receive their treatment once every 3 weeks for up to 10 years. They will also receive other drugs to relieve adverse effects.

Biopsies, blood tests, and imaging scans will be repeated during some study visits. Participants may also have urine tests and tests of their heart function.

Participants may remain in the study as long as the treatment is helping them. If they stop treatment, they will have safety visits 14, 30, and 90 days after their last dose. Additional follow-up visits will continue 5 to 10 years.

trials.conds: Metastatic Colorectal Cancer; Metastatic Pancreatic Cancer; Metastatic Ovarian Cancer; Metastatic Breast Carcinoma; Metastatic Endocrine Tumors/ Neuroendocrine Tumors
trials.brief:
Background:

The NCI Surgery Branch has developed an experimental therapy that involves taking white blood cells from patients' tumors, growing them in the laboratory in large numbers, and then giving the cells back to the patient. These cells are called Tumor Infiltrating Lymphocytes, or TIL and we have given this type of treatment to over 200 patients with melanoma. Researchers want to know if TIL shrink s tumors in people with digestive tract, urothelial, breast, or ovarian/endometrial cancers. In this study, we are selecting a specific subset of white blood cells from the tumor that we think are the most effective in fighting tumors and will use only these cells in making the tumor fighting cells.

Objective:

The purpose of this study is to see if these specifically selected tumor fighting cells can cause digestive tract, urothelial, breast, or ovarian/endometrial tumors to shrink and to see if this treatment is safe.

Eligibility:

\- Adults age 18-72 with upper or lower gastrointestinal, hepatobiliary, genitourinary, breast, ovarian/endometrial cancer, or glioblastoma refractory to standard chemotherapy.

Design:

Work up stage: Patients will be seen as an outpatient at the NIH clinical Center and undergo a history and physical examination, scans, x-rays, lab tests, and other tests as needed.

Surgery: If the patients meet all of the requirements for the study they will undergo surgery to remove a tumor that can be used to grow the TIL product.

Leukapheresis: Patients may undergo leukapheresis to obtain additional white blood cells. (Leukapheresis is a common procedure, which removes only the white blood cells from the patient.)

Treatment: Once their cells have grown, the patients will be admitted to the hospital for the conditioning chemotherapy, the TIL cells and aldesleukin. They will stay in the hospital for about 4 weeks for the treatment.

Follow up: Patients will return to the clinic for a physical exam, review of side effects, lab tests, and scans about every 1-3 months for the first year, and then every 6 months to 1 year as long as their tumors are shrinking. Follow up visits will take up to 2 days.

This clinical trial uses a study drug (NP-101) alone in some parts of the study or with a recommended treatment for GEP-NEC called Nivo/Ipi (a combination of Nivolumab and Ipilimumab) in other parts of the study and tests it against Placebo (look alike capsules with no active drug) with Nivo/Ipi. The study is divided into three parts. Participants will participate in only one of 3 study parts: Part 1- Dose escalation or Part 2 - Dose selection or Part 3 - Selected dose continuation.

The goal of this clinical trial is to learn if NP-101 (the study drug) can help people with poorly differentiated GEP-NEC live longer; the study includes males and females, age 18 and older who agree to join the study and who qualify.

The main questions the study seeks to answer:

1. Is the study drug in combination with Nivo/Ipi safe?
2. How does the body process the study drug alone and in combination with Nivo/Ipi?
3. How does the body process the study drug with and without food?

Participants will be asked to report how they are feeling, allow for blood draws, body scans, visit the clinic for testing, allow for removal of tumor tissue, take study drug or capsules without medication (along with the recommended treatment) and other procedures which will be explained, along with the study visit schedule, in detail by the study staff before agreeing to participate.

trials.brief:
Background:

\- Skin disease can have many causes. It can have widespread consequences, and in rare cases can lead to death. Researchers want to determine the causes of various types of skin diseases and find a way to treat them.

Objectives:

\- To determine the causes of various skin diseases and find ways to treat them.

Eligibility:

* People ages 2 and older who have:

  * A skin disease or at risk of developing a skin disease OR
  * A family member of persons with a skin disease
* Healthy volunteers ages 2 and older

Design:

* Participants will be screened under a separate protocol.
* Participants may take a survey about how their skin condition affects their quality of life.
* Participants will have a medical history and a physical exam including a detailed skin exam. Pictures will be taken of their skin to document any skin disease.
* Participants will have specimens collected. This may include:

  * Several teaspoons of blood taken at each visit
  * Stool samples
  * Nail and body fluid (like saliva) samples
  * Cheek swabs. The inside of the cheek will be scraped for about a minute in each direction to collect cells.
  * Collection of skin samples with:

    * A swab (like a Q-tip)
    * Gently scraping skin to remove the outer layers of cells
    * Applying and removing 1-inch pieces of tape
* Participants may have up to 4 skin biopsies in 12 months, with 4 separate biopsies taken each time.

  * An area of skin will be numbed with an injection.
  * A piece of skin the size of a pencil eraser will be removed using a small instrument.
  * A flat scar usually develops at the biopsy site.

trials.brief:
Neuroendocrine tumours (NETs) are slow growing cancers, which commonly present as metastatic incurable disease. Some neuroendocrine tumours, termed functional NETs, overproduce hormones which result in a variety of symptoms. However, approximately 75% of NETs are considered non-functional meaning that they do not result in hormone overproduction. The main treatment for both functional and non-functional NETs is somatostatin analogues (SSA, a type of inhibitory hormone). These drugs slow tumour growth and reduce hormone production. Over time, the majority of patients will experience tumour growth despite treatment with SSA therapy. When this occurs, the addition of Peptide Receptor Radionuclide Therapy (PRRT, a type of targeted radiotherapy) in combination with ongoing SSA therapy is given. However, it is not known if continuing SSA therapy after commencement of PRRT is beneficial or not.

The aim of this study is to estimate the outcomes of patients with grade 1 and 2 well differentiated mid, hind-gut or pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours who have progressed on SSA therapy and receive subsequent PRRT with or without concurrent SSA.

trials.title: Testing the Safety and Effectiveness of Radiation-based Treatment (Lutetium Lu 177 Dotatate) for Metastatic Prostate Cancer That Has Neuroendocrine Cells
trials.conds: Metastatic Prostate Adenocarcinoma With Neuroendocrine Differentiation; Metastatic Prostate Neuroendocrine Carcinoma; Metastatic Prostate Small Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma; Stage IVB Prostate Cancer AJCC v8
trials.interventions: Biospecimen Collection; Computed Tomography; Gallium Ga 68-DOTATATE; Lutetium Lu 177 Dotatate
trials.brief: This phase II trial studies how well lutetium Lu 177 dotatate works in treating patients with prostate cancer with neuroendocrine differentiation that has spread to other places in the body (metastatic). Neuroendocrine differentiation refers to cells that have traits of both hormone-producing endocrine cells and nerve cells. These cells release hormones into the blood in response to a signal from the nervous system. Hormones are biological substances that circulate through the bloodstream to control the activity of other organs or cells in the body. Lutetium Lu 177-dotatate is a radioactive drug. It binds to a protein called somatostatin receptor, which is found on some neuroendocrine tumor cells. Lutetium Lu 177-dotatate builds up in these cells and gives off radiation that may kill them. It is a type of radioconjugate and a type of somatostatin analog. Treatment with Lutetium Lu 177 dotatate may shrink the tumor in a way that can be measured in patients with metastatic prostate cancer with neuroendocrine differentiation.

trials.title: Evaluating the Addition of the Immunotherapy Drug Atezolizumab to Standard Chemotherapy Treatment for Advanced or Metastatic Neuroendocrine Carcinomas That Originate Outside the Lung
trials.conds: Advanced Extrapulmonary Neuroendocrine Carcinoma; Metastatic Extrapulmonary Neuroendocrine Carcinoma; Recurrent Extrapulmonary Neuroendocrine Carcinoma; Unresectable Extrapulmonary Neuroendocrine Carcinoma
trials.brief: This phase II/III trial compares the effect of immunotherapy with atezolizumab in combination with standard chemotherapy with a platinum drug (cisplatin or carboplatin) and etoposide versus standard therapy alone for the treatment of poorly differentiated extrapulmonary (originated outside the lung) neuroendocrine cancer that may have spread from where it first started to nearby tissue, lymph nodes, or distant parts of the body (advanced) or that has spread from where it first started (primary site) to other places in the body (metastatic). The other aim of this trial is to compare using atezolizumab just at the beginning of treatment versus continuing it beyond the initial treatment. Immunotherapy with monoclonal antibodies, such as atezolizumab, may help the body's immune system attack the cancer, and may interfere with the ability of tumor cells to grow and spread. Cisplatin and carboplatin are in a class of medications known as platinum-containing compounds that work by killing, stopping or slowing the growth of cancer cells. Etoposide is in a class of medications known as podophyllotoxin derivatives. It blocks a certain enzyme needed for cell division and DNA repair, and it may kill cancer cells. Giving atezolizumab in combination with a platinum drug (cisplatin or carboplatin) and etoposide may work better in treating patients with poorly differentiated extrapulmonary neuroendocrine cancer compared to standard therapy with a platinum drug (cisplatin or carboplatin) and etoposide alone.

Giving cabozantinib, nivolumab, and ipilimumab may work better in treating patients with genitourinary tumors that have no treatment options compared to giving cabozantinib, nivolumab, or ipilimumab alone.

trials.title: DAREON®-NEC-1: A Study in People With Advanced Extrapulmonary Neuroendocrine Cancer (epNEC) to Compare Obrixtamig Plus Carboplatin and Etoposide Treatment With Standard Chemotherapy
trials.conds: Extrapulmonary Neuroendocrine Cancer (epNEC)
trials.interventions: Obrixtamig; Carboplatin; Etoposide; Ventana DLL3 RxDx assay
trials.brief:
This study is open to adults with advanced extrapulmonary neuroendocrine cancer. The purpose of this study is to find out if a study medicine called obrixtamig plus standard chemotherapy (carboplatin and etoposide) improves survival when compared to standard chemotherapy (carboplatin and etoposide) alone. Obrixtamig is an antibody-like molecule that may help the immune system fight cancer. Another purpose of the study is to test a medical device being developed to measure levels of the tumour marker delta-like ligand 3 (DLL3).

Participants are put into 2 groups randomly, which means by chance. One group (treatment arm) receives obrixtamig and standard chemotherapy followed by obrixtamig alone for up to 3 years. The other group (control arm) receives standard chemotherapy without obrixtamig for about 4 months. All treatments are given as infusions into a vein.

During the study, participants in both groups visit the study site regularly. Participants in the treatment arm stay overnight at the study site following the first 2 obrixtamig treatments. The doctors regularly check participants' health and take note of any unwanted effects. At some of the visits, doctors check the size of the tumour(s). The results are compared between the 2 groups to see whether the treatment works.

trials.title: DAREON®-36: A Study to Test Obrixtamig in Combination With ZL-1310 in People With Advanced Small Cell Lung Cancer or Other Neuroendocrine Cancers
trials.conds: Small Cell Lung Cancer; Large Cell Neuroendocrine Lung Carcinoma; Extrapulmonary Neuroendocrine Carcinoma of Small Cell Histology; Extrapulmonary Neuroendocrine Carcinoma of Large Cell Histology
trials.brief:
This study is open to adults with advanced small cell lung cancer and other neuroendocrine cancers. The study has 2 parts. The purpose of Part 1 is to find a suitable dose of a combination study treatment, obrixtamig and ZL-1310. The purpose of Part 2 is to see how obrixtamig and ZL-1310 is tolerated when given with another medicine called a checkpoint inhibitor. Another purpose is to check whether the study treatment can stop the cancer from growing and keep it stable. Obrixtamig and ZL-1310 are being developed to help the immune system fight cancer.

In Part 1, participants get obrixtamig and ZL-1310. In Part 2, participants get obrixtamig and ZL-1310 with a checkpoint inhibitor. Part 2 is only open to people with advanced small cell lung cancer. All study treatments are given as infusions into a vein.

The study does not have a fixed duration. Participants can receive study treatment for up to 2 years if they benefit from treatment and can tolerate it. Participants visit the study site regularly, with some overnight stays required. During this time, doctors regularly check for health problems that could be caused by the study treatment. They also monitor the size of the tumour(s) and take laboratory tests.

trials.title: Randomized Trial of Topotecan With M6620, an ATR Kinase Inhibitor, in Small Cell Lung Cancers and Small Cell Cancers Outside of the Lungs
trials.conds: Extensive Stage Lung Small Cell Carcinoma; Extrapulmonary Small Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma; Limited Stage Lung Small Cell Carcinoma; Platinum-Resistant Lung Small Cell Carcinoma; Platinum-Sensitive Lung Small Cell Carcinoma; Recurrent Lung Small Cell Carcinoma
trials.interventions: Berzosertib; Biopsy Procedure; Biospecimen Collection; Computed Tomography
trials.brief: This phase II trial studies how well berzosertib (M6620) works when given in combination with topotecan hydrochloride (topotecan) compared with topotecan alone in treating patients with small cell lung cancer that has come back (relapsed), or small cell cancer that arises from a site other than the lung (extrapulmonary). Drugs used in chemotherapy, such as topotecan hydrochloride, work by damaging the DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) in tumor cells, causing those cells to die and the tumor to shrink. However, some tumor cells can become less affected by chemotherapy because they have ways to repair the damaged DNA. The addition of M6620 could help topotecan hydrochloride shrink the cancer and prevent it from returning by blocking enzymes needed for DNA repair.
